title: One trait a week
hook: Mendel of Satanov adapted Benjamin Franklin's method in 1812

segments.voice: Yesterday's word: cheshbon hanefesh, an accounting of the soul. Your line was account for the soul. Did you give the day its two honest minutes? Today, a way to keep that ledger week after week. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

Benjamin Franklin, in his autobiography, describes a small notebook. One page for each virtue he wanted. A column for each day of the week. Each day he made a little black mark wherever he had slipped. And he didn't try to fix everything at once. He gave each virtue a week of close attention, then moved to the next, the way, he says, a gardener weeds one bed at a time instead of the whole garden. A Jewish writer in Eastern Europe, Mendel of Satanov, read about that notebook. What he did next is today's lesson.
screen: `A PAGE FOR EACH VIRTUE.` → `A BLACK MARK FOR EACH SLIP.` → `ONE BED AT A TIME.`

segments.voice: One trait a week. Four pieces to it. First, the borrowing. Mendel of Satanov wrote a Hebrew book called Cheshbon HaNefesh, named for yesterday's word. In it he laid out a method for working on character that, as historians describe it, he adapted from Franklin's notebook. He didn't copy it whole. He chose his own list of traits, and gave each one a Hebrew name and a short line to carry, and wrote it for Jewish readers. A good tool, found in an unexpected place, put to work in his own house. Second, the list. His traits are middot, measures, and several of them are coming in the days ahead: humility, patience, order, calm of soul, silence. You will meet each one by name. Third, the week. The method is simple on purpose. Pick one trait. For one week, it gets your full attention: you say its short line, you watch for it during the day, and at night, in your accounting, you mark where it slipped. The other traits aren't abandoned; they just wait their turn. Then the next week, the next trait. When the list is done, you go around again. Fourth, why one. Try to become patient, humble, orderly and calm all by Friday, and it's easy to lose track of all four by Wednesday. Give one trait seven days, the method hopes, and it starts to show up on its own, in the checkout line and the group chat. Mendel's gift was making it fit in a pocket: one page, one trait, one week.
screen: `A TOOL BORROWED AND MADE HIS OWN.` · `A LIST OF MIDDOT, EACH WITH A LINE.` · `ONE TRAIT GETS THE WHOLE WEEK.` · `ONE, SO IT ACTUALLY SHOWS UP.` · then, large: `ONE TRAIT A WEEK.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pick one trait for a week. Settle, and breathe. Let a few traits pass through your mind: patience, honesty, order, calm, generosity, quiet. Notice which one tugs at you, the one this week actually needs. Choose it. Now give it a short line of your own, a few plain words you could say at a red light. Then picture one place this week where it will be tested: a meeting, a commute, a dinner. See yourself there with the trait in your pocket. If you pray, you can ask God's help with it, in your own words. If you don't, simply hold the choice. The bell holds the time.
One trait a week. Mendel of Satanov's method, adapted from Benjamin Franklin's notebook: one middah gets a whole week of attention, with a short line and a nightly mark. Today's word.
Your line: one trait a week. Write today's trait somewhere you'll see it, on a sticky note or your lock screen, and make one mark for it tonight. Day one thousand two hundred fifty-five.

howItsDone: In Mussar groups that follow Mendel of Satanov's Cheshbon HaNefesh, people focus on one trait for a week, repeat a short phrase for it, and note each evening where it slipped, then move to the next trait on the list.

fork.setup: you're a Jewish writer, and you've read about a statesman's notebook for working on virtues, one at a time. what do you do?
options: ignore it; it isn't from a Jewish book.
adapt it: your own list of middot, in Hebrew, for Jewish readers.
fork.reveal: Mendel of Satanov made the method his own, with his own list of traits and a short line for each, in a book he named Cheshbon HaNefesh.

notes: Outline hook gives the year 1812; under the claims rule the year is left out. Add it back only if a reviewer confirms the publication date of Cheshbon HaNefesh.

Franklin's notebook (a page per virtue, days in columns, black marks, a week per virtue, the gardener weeding one bed at a time) is paraphrased from his Autobiography; confirm details. The number of virtues is left out on purpose.
That Mendel adapted Franklin's method is attributed ('as historians describe it'); confirm and check whether the book names Franklin.
The lesson says the coming days' traits (humility, patience, order, calm of soul, silence) are on Mendel's list; confirm each appears in Cheshbon HaNefesh.
'Each trait has a short line' describes the book's short phrase per trait; confirm.

Editor pass: Franklin marks 'each day', not 'every evening' (closer to the Autobiography); Mendel Lefin called a Jewish writer, not a rabbi; dropped the claim that his list was 'met earlier this week'; softened the promise that one week makes a trait show up; varied the teach opener.
